for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL','pypdfium2']:
 print(name, importlib.util.find_spec(name))

PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(reader.pages))
for i,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
 text=p.extract_text()
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i} ===\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1)))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/page-01.txt').read_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper identifies a useful limitation of fixed agent-count curricula: increasing the number of agents can improve reward availability without making the resulting policy more useful for the target task. Adapting the curriculum in either direction is well motivated.

SPMARL is a simple, practical combination of self-paced context optimization and critic-based task prioritization. The comparison with SPRLM, using the same hyperparameters, provides a useful control for the change in curriculum objective.

The empirical evaluation is substantial: Simple-Spread, the 20-player XOR game, eight SMACv2 scenarios, and two dense-reward BenchMARL tasks. Table 1 reports meaningful improvements over SPRLM on Simple-Spread and the harder Protoss tasks, supporting the practical promise of the approach.

Curriculum trajectories, target-task evaluations, reported five-seed confidence intervals, significance tests, and the threshold ablation help assess the results. Pseudocode, implementation notes, hyperparameter tables, and a source-code link also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as policy improvement is insufficiently supported. Equation 4 measures prediction error, which mixes critic approximation error with variability in returns; it does not directly measure improvement or even policy change. An accurately evaluated policy can remain suboptimal, and stochastic tasks can retain substantial loss without offering useful learning progress. The paper neither validates this proxy against subsequent policy improvement nor directly measures the claimed reduction in credit-assignment difficulty.

The variance analysis does not establish the proposed explanation. Appendix A.3.4 computes dispersion across approximately 25 different sampled contexts, which combines genuine task differences with estimation noise. Figures 7 and 10 also compare returns against averaged squared residuals under different training processes. These quantities differ in scale and temporal aggregation, so smaller standard deviation does not demonstrate more reliable estimation. A comparison using matched policies, contexts, and sampling budgets is needed to support this principal claim.

The relationship to closely related work is incomplete. Prioritized Level Replay (Jiang et al., ICML 2021) already uses value-error-based scores to prioritize training environments. Discussing only transition-level prioritized replay misses a particularly relevant precedent. Combining such prioritization with SPRL and agent-count control can still constitute a contribution, but its distinct contribution needs clearer positioning and an appropriate comparison.

Some baseline choices limit the conclusions. Simple-Spread uses an increasing Linear curriculum even though the paper explicitly explains why that direction is unsuitable; a decreasing or performance-triggered schedule would be more informative. Moreover, the paper attributes ALPGMM and VACL failures partly to their lack of convergence toward the target distribution, but does not test whether adding comparable target-task training closes the gap. The SPRLM comparison helps isolate the objective change, but does not resolve these broader comparison issues.

The implemented learning-progress statistic is ambiguous. Equation 4 defines its target as a discounted return, whereas Appendix A.3.4 describes a one-step bootstrapped target, and the MAPPO description introduces GAE. These alternatives can produce different task rankings. The manuscript should specify the exact target, normalization, aggregation, and timing relative to critic updates. It should also clarify whether SMAC performance thresholds apply to win rate or the stated signed terminal returns.

Claims of consistently surpassing all baselines exceed the reported evidence. Table 2 finds no significant advantage over SPRLM on XOR or Protoss 5v5, and none over ALPGMM on Protoss 5v5 or 6v6; the dense-reward tasks show comparable performance. The evidence supports competitive performance with gains on several sparse-reward tasks, while the broader superiority and mechanistic claims remain insufficiently established.
